newsitem.title: ITALY: Talks on future of Bosnian town Brcko open in Rome.
newsitem.headline: Talks on future of Bosnian town Brcko open in Rome.

text.p: International talks on the disputed north Bosnian town of Brcko opened in Rome on Wednesday, diplomatic sources said.

The talks, chaired by U.S. lawyer Roberts Owen and due to last until Saturday, take place against a backdrop of increasingly tough rhetoric from rival Serb and Moslem leaders over the future of the narrow and militarily vital corridor.
Brcko, a Sava river port linking Serb-held land to the west and east, is seen as the most volatile flashpoint in Bosnia.

The first session is supposed to give both sides a chance to present evidence to the arbitration panel made up of Owen, Cazim Sadikovic of the Moslem-Croat federation and Vitomir Popovic of the Serb republic.
Similar attempts to begin international arbitration over Brcko have collapsed with the Bosnian Serb side refusing to attend meetings.
But Colum Murphy, a spokesman for the office of the High Representative to Bosnia, said in Sarajevo on Tuesday that the Serb delegation had promised to participate.
No one directly involved with the talks could immediately be reached for comment and it was not immediately clear whether the Bosnian Serb side had kept its promise.

A peace agreement that ended the Bosnian war a year ago failed to resolve the future status of Brcko, which separatist Serb forces seized early in the 43-month-long conflict after expelling the Moslem and Croat population.

Bosnian Serb leaders insist Brcko must remain under the control of the country's Serb republic and have warned they will go to war to protect what they consider to be a lifeline for Serb-held territory.
The Bosnian Serb member of Bosnia's collective presidency, Momcilo Krajisnik, told Bosnian Serb radio on Wednesday that losing control of Brcko could lead to war.
He said that for the Serbs, losing Brcko would be like "losing the entire Bosnian Serb Republic.
"We would be compelled to wage war if someone attacked us with the intention of severing this link between the two parts of the republic," Krajisnik said.
"We would not move out of the western or eastern part, we would go to war over Brcko."
Moslem-Croat federation leaders have rejected the Serb threats and say their legal arguments -- based on the town's mixed pre-war population -- will prevail in the arbitration.
The Brcko talks were the top item on the main evening news of Moslem-controlled Bosnian state radio in Sarajevo.
"We hope justice will prevail and we'll get Brcko back," a Moslem woman living in federation territory near Brcko told the radio in an interview.
"Moslems were in the highest number there before the war. We have got nothing against Serbs living there with us again."
The Dayton peace treaty originally set December 14, 1996 as the deadline for resolving Brcko but the parties postponed the deadline until February 15.
Under the Dayton accords, Bosnia is preserved as a loose union divided into autonomous Serb and Moslem-Croat entities.
